title: Product-Market Fit: The 5 Signals That Tell You If You Actually Have It
description: Everyone says they're working toward product-market fit. Here's how PMs measure it—5 signals, benchmarks, and what to do when data is mixed.
body:
# Product-Market Fit: The 5 Signals That Tell You If You Actually Have It

Everyone says they're working toward product-market fit. Almost nobody agrees on what it actually looks like when you have it.

Marc Andreessen's original definition — "being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market" — is true but not useful for a PM trying to decide whether to scale distribution or keep iterating on the core product. You need something you can measure.

Here are the five signals that actually tell you whether you have product-market fit, and what to do when the evidence is mixed.

## Why Vanity Metrics Lie About PMF

The most common PMF mistake is using top-of-funnel metrics as evidence. "We have 10,000 sign-ups" says nothing about fit. Sign-ups measure the strength of your acquisition channel, not the quality of your product-market match. A well-targeted ad campaign or a Product Hunt launch can generate thousands of sign-ups for a product that nobody actually uses.

PMF lives in retention, not acquisition. The question isn't "how many people tried us?" It's "of the people who tried us, how many found something they couldn't live without?"

## Signal 1: The Sean Ellis Score (40% Rule)

The most widely cited quantitative PMF benchmark comes from Sean Ellis, who surveyed users at dozens of SaaS companies and found that companies with strong PMF had at least 40% of their users answer "very disappointed" when asked: *"How would you feel if you could no longer use this product?"*

The survey is three questions:
1. How would you feel if you could no longer use [product]? (Very disappointed / Somewhat disappointed / Not disappointed / N/A — I've stopped using it)
2. What type of person do you think would most benefit from [product]?
3. What is the primary benefit you receive from [product]?

This is not a satisfaction survey. It's a disappointment survey, and the distinction matters. Satisfaction can be gamed by delightful onboarding or responsive support. Disappointment at losing the product measures genuine dependency.

If you're below 40%, the qualitative data from questions 2 and 3 tells you who does have a strong reaction (your core PMF segment) and what they value most. This is the data that drives your next product iteration — not the aggregate score.

## Signal 2: Retention Curves That Flatten

For most product categories, the gold standard PMF evidence is a retention curve that flattens at a meaningful level rather than declining toward zero.

Every cohort loses some users over time — that's expected. What you're looking for is a cohort that hits a floor and stays there. In consumer apps, a retention floor of 20-30% at the 12-week mark is a strong PMF signal for most categories. In B2B SaaS, the equivalent metric is often annual renewal rate — companies with genuine PMF renew at 85%+ even before expansion.

### The Smiling Retention Curve

One advanced pattern worth knowing: occasionally, well-designed products show retention that rises after an initial drop, forming a smile shape. This happens when the product has a ramp-up period — users who stick through the learning curve become highly retained advocates. If you see this shape in your cohort data, you have a UX problem (hard to get started) masking a PMF signal (deeply valuable once adopted). Fix the onboarding, don't pivot the product.

## Signal 3: Organic Word-of-Mouth at Scale

The Superhuman PMF study, led by Rahul Vohra, added a powerful dimension to Ellis's framework: segment your "very disappointed" users and look at who they say the product is for. The segment that gives you both the highest disappointment score AND an accurate, specific description of the ideal user is your PMF core.

The tactical implication: after you identify that core segment, measure their referral behavior specifically. PMF users refer. Not-quite-PMF users don't. If your highest-satisfaction segment isn't referring, the product may be delivering value that feels good but isn't solving a problem painful enough to make someone go out of their way to recommend it.

Organic word-of-mouth — referrals you didn't pay for, reviews you didn't ask for, social mentions you didn't prompt — is the strongest leading indicator of sustainable growth. Track it by acquisition source and watch whether your organic channel is growing as a percentage of new users, not just in absolute numbers.

## Signal 4: Usage Depth and the Aha Moment Completion Rate

PMF users use the product differently than non-PMF users. They reach deeper features. They come back without prompting. They set up integrations. They invite colleagues.

The metric to watch is **aha moment completion rate**: what percentage of new users reach the specific moment in your product that correlates with long-term retention? For Slack, it was sending 2,000 messages. For Dropbox, it was adding at least one file to a folder. For LinkedIn, it was reaching a certain number of connections.

To find your aha moment:
1. Take your best-retained cohort (users still active at 90 days)
2. Compare their first-week behavior to churned users' first-week behavior
3. Find the action or sequence that strongly predicts retention vs. churn
4. That's your aha moment

Once you know it, aha moment completion rate in the first week becomes your most actionable leading indicator of PMF. If it's rising, you're moving toward fit. If it's flat despite feature releases, your changes aren't reaching the core problem.

## Signal 5: Customers Demanding the Product Back After Cancellation

This one is qualitative, but it's the most visceral PMF signal: what happens when customers cancel or when you have an outage?

Products with genuine PMF generate inbound when they go down. Customers email, tweet, and call your support line — not to complain, but because they need to know when the product will be back. Cancellation conversations turn into negotiations rather than confirmations.

If customers cancel and simply leave, you have a usage problem. If customers cancel and immediately ask about the roadmap or whether a specific feature is coming, you have a timing problem (they need something you haven't built yet). If they cancel and never look back, you have a PMF problem.

Listen to cancel conversations with the same rigor you apply to quantitative cohort analysis.

## When the Signals Are Mixed

In practice, most product teams see a mixed picture: strong retention in one segment, weak retention broadly; high Ellis scores from power users, indifferent scores from casual users; strong word-of-mouth in one channel but low organic growth overall.

Mixed signals almost always mean you have PMF in a narrow segment but haven't yet identified how to reach more people who match that profile, or you're trying to serve too broad a market simultaneously.

**The correct response to mixed signals is to narrow, not to iterate.** Find the segment showing the strongest PMF evidence, describe them precisely (not "SMBs" but "B2B SaaS founders with 5-30 engineers who've raised a Series A and are running marketing without a dedicated team"), and focus all acquisition and product energy on that cohort until the signals are unambiguous.

PM teams that broaden when signals are mixed typically delay finding fit for 6-12 months while chasing a bigger addressable market.

## Connecting PMF Measurement to Your Roadmap

PMF is not a binary state you achieve once. It's a continuous measurement that should inform every roadmap prioritization decision.

Before adding a new feature, ask: will this increase retention and engagement in the segment showing the strongest fit, or will it serve a new segment that hasn't shown evidence of fit yet? The first is expansion within a proven model. The second is a bet on a new hypothesis — which can be right, but needs to be sized accordingly.

The [RICE prioritization framework](/learn) becomes much more precise when "impact" is specifically defined as "impact on retention and engagement for our core PMF segment" rather than "impact on DAU." Link your prioritization to the PMF signals, and your roadmap becomes a theory about how to deepen fit — not just a feature list.

## Practicing PMF Thinking

Understanding PMF conceptually is the first step. Applying it under pressure — in an interview, in a product review, in a funding conversation — requires practice.

[PM Streak's daily challenges](/daily-challenge) include PMF diagnosis cases where you're given real product data and asked to identify whether the evidence supports scaling or continued iteration. The [interview prep section](/interview-prep) covers the PMF questions that show up in senior PM interviews at growth-stage companies.

The PMs who can look at a retention curve, an Ellis score, and a set of cancellation notes and synthesize a clear recommendation are the ones getting promoted. Build that skill through deliberate repetition, not through reading about it once.
